analysis.one_liner: Bars U.S. trade officials from supporting any waiver of COVID-19 vaccine and treatment patents at the WTO.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Tim Scott with 3 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut off funding for the U.S. Trade Representative if the office supported, allowed, or facilitated any World Trade Organization measure to waive intellectual property rights on COVID-19 vaccines and treatments — including the waiver proposed by India and South Africa that would let other countries make affordable generic versions. Supporters argued strong patents are what drove rapid vaccine development and that waiving them could hand technology to China. Opponents argued the waiver was needed to expand global vaccine production and end the pandemic faster. The bill was referred to the Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name pharmaceutical and vaccine companies benefit most: the bill would lock in U.S. government opposition to any relaxation of their exclusive patent rights on COVID-19 vaccines and treatments, preserving monopoly pricing and blocking the proposed WTO waiver. The bill's findings also frame the measure as protecting U.S. biotech leadership against foreign competitors.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any funds available to the U.S. Trade Representative from being used to support, allow, or facilitate the negotiation or approval of the India–South Africa WTO waiver for COVID-19 vaccines and treatments, or any other WTO intellectual-property waiver.

States the sense of Congress that the United States should keep promoting strong international intellectual property rights and oppose transferring U.S. intellectual property to China or other countries.

analysis.who_pays: People in developing countries would bear the main cost, since a U.S. ban on supporting the waiver would make it much harder to approve generic production of COVID-19 vaccines and treatments. Americans pay indirectly too: a slower global rollout prolongs the pandemic, which means more infections, more disruptions, and a larger pool for new variants. Generic manufacturers, largely in India and South Africa, would also lose the chance to produce low-cost versions.
analysis.who_pays_short: People in poorer countries awaiting vaccines

drawbacks.text: The bill would tie the hands of U.S. trade negotiators in an active WTO negotiation during a global pandemic, ruling out a tool that many public health experts said was needed to expand vaccine manufacturing in poorer countries.

The bill's own findings concede the goal of the proposed waiver was to help with the 'prevention, containment, and treatment of COVID-19'; blocking it means patent exclusivity stays ahead of pandemic containment as a policy priority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs almost entirely to brand-name vaccine and drug makers, which keep exclusive patent rights and monopoly pricing on COVID-19 products. The cost falls on global pandemic response: fewer affordable generic vaccines and treatments in poorer countries, a longer pandemic, and more variant risk for everyone, including Americans. The bill's counter-argument — that patents drove the rapid innovation behind the vaccines and that a waiver could weaken future incentives — is a genuine one, but the bill went further than defending patents case-by-case: it barred U.S. support for any WTO IP waiver at all, even after the emergency, with no exception for a negotiated compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, joined by Senators Toomey, Grassley, and Burr.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its last action of the Congress.
The bill had 3 cosponsors, all Republicans, out of 50 Senate Republicans.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the COVID-19 vaccine patent waiver — led by India and South Africa, along with generic drug manufacturers and global public health advocates — are better off, because the U.S. Trade Representative was never legally barred from supporting a waiver at the WTO. Brand-name vaccine makers gained nothing permanent, since the bill did not pass; they simply kept the patent position they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wavier supporters and generic drug makers

for.name: Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar U.S. support for any WTO waiver of COVID-19 intellectual property rights.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Biden administration (U.S. Trade Representative)
against.what_they_did: Announced in May 2021 that the United States would support negotiating a waiver of intellectual property protections for COVID-19 vaccines at the WTO, putting the administration on the opposite side of the bill's core purpose.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans (1 sponsor plus 3 of 50 Senate Republicans), and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never acted on the bill; the Democratic administration also favored the WTO waiver the bill was designed to block.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and vaccine makers (including mRNA vaccine producers)
industries.note: The bill would have committed the U.S. government to opposing any WTO waiver of their patents on COVID-19 vaccines and treatments, preserving monopoly pricing and blocking generic competition worldwide. Its interest runs against cheaper, faster vaccine access for ordinary people in the U.S. and abroad.

industries.industry: Generic drug manufacturers (concentrated in India, South Africa, and other middle-income countries)
industries.note: The bill targets exactly the waiver these manufacturers sought, which would have let them produce low-cost generic COVID-19 vaccines and treatments. Their interest in the bill runs alongside the public's interest in wider access.
